summary: Poses open questions about path-aware networking, where endpoints can see properties of available paths and choose among them. Some of this exists within single domains already, while a fully path-aware internetwork would extend it across layers and the Internet. It is informational.

eli5.summary: What if travelers could see all roads and pick their own? This lists the puzzles still to solve.

questions: open questions in path selection by endpoints
how do endpoints discover network paths
why should endpoints choose their own paths
subtitle: Research questions about letting endpoints see and choose network paths

tldr.problem: Today, endpoints cannot see what paths their traffic takes through the Internet or choose among them. This research document poses questions about how to design a path-aware Internet where endpoints can discover path properties and select paths.
tldr.mechanism: It identifies eight research questions: defining path properties, distributing them trustworthily, enabling path selection, creating interfaces between layers, redesigning transport protocols, handling different endpoint types, operating path-aware networks, and managing the transition from today's architecture.
tldr.outcome: Informational: these questions frame ongoing research in the Path Aware Networking Research Group and are open as of 2021. No answers or designs are proposed.

today: RFC 9217 is informational and has not been obsoleted. It represents the consensus of PANRG as of 2021 about the open questions in path-aware internetworking. The questions remain active research topics in the community.

sections.title: Path-Aware Networking Today and Tomorrow
sections.content:
The current Internet works like a one-way radio dispatch system: endpoints send packets to a destination address and trust the network to route them. Endpoints have no way to see what path their traffic takes, no guarantee about the properties of that path (speed, latency, loss, or node visibility), and no ability to choose among paths.

Path-aware networking flips this: endpoints can discover the properties of available paths and select which path their traffic should use. This property already exists within single domains (one organization's network) and through administrative tools, but a fully path-aware Internet would extend it across domain boundaries and make it available to applications and end users.

The document poses eight open research questions that must be answered to realize a path-aware Internet, framing discussions within the Path Aware Networking Research Group.
sections.eli5: Right now the network is like a mailbox: you drop a letter in and hope it gets there. Path-aware means the letter could pick a faster route, a safer route, or whichever one it wants.

sections.title: What Is a Path?
sections.content:
The document defines a path as a sequence of adjacent path elements over which a packet can travel. The definition remains deliberately abstract because answering the first research questions will refine what counts as a path element.

A path property is information about a path, such as whether a specific service node is on it (relatively static) or current latency and loss rates (dynamic). Path properties may apply to a single element, the whole path, or a subpath.

In this model, path-aware networking means endpoints can discover path properties and react to them by selecting or influencing paths for their traffic, regardless of whether this works through protocol features at the network, transport, or application layer.
sections.eli5: A path is the route a packet takes. Path properties are facts about that route: is it fast or slow, does it go through a particular place, will packets get lost?

sections.title: Eight Questions
sections.content:
Question 1: Path Vocabulary. How are paths and their properties defined and represented? The answer must balance expressiveness (details about path components) against scalability and privacy (exposing all node-level topology publicly may conflict with network operators' business goals).

Question 2: Discovery and Trust. How do endpoints and applications get accurate, trustworthy information about path properties? Methods could be in-band or out-of-band, push or pull. Temporal issues arise with dynamic properties: by the time a property measurement reaches an endpoint, the path may have changed.

Question 3: Path Selection. How can endpoints select paths trustworthily, such that the outcome is predictable and no worse than using a single path? This requires choices about granularity (per packet, per flow, per aggregate) and what information to expose (path properties or path identities).

Question 4: Layering. How can network, transport, and application layers expose path information and selection interfaces to each other? Applications need defaults and sensible options, while still supporting fine-grained per-path control when needed.

Question 5: Transport and Application Design. How should protocols above the network layer adapt when traffic on a single flow can traverse different paths at different times? For example, if packets are sprayed across paths to resist surveillance, higher-layer protocols must avoid using linkable identifiers across paths.

Question 6: Diverse Endpoints. How do path-awareness concepts differ when applied to gateways and tunnel endpoints (which handle traffic between domains) versus application endpoints? Gateways may receive and use different path information than end devices.

Question 7: Network Operations. How can operators manage a path-aware network when endpoints make their own path choices? Conflicts may arise between routing decisions by the network and path selection by endpoints; safety principles are needed to ensure connectivity is not degraded.

Question 8: Deployment Transition. How can the Internet transition from path-oblivious to path-aware operation? Network operators must be incentivized to give up some control, and the dynamics of early deployment (when few endpoints use path selection) may differ from mature deployment.
sections.eli5: The eight questions in order: (1) What are paths and how do we describe them? (2) How do endpoints learn about paths? (3) How do they pick one? (4) How do layers talk to each other about paths? (5) How do TCP and apps need to change? (6) Do gateways work differently than user devices? (7) How does an operator keep things running? (8) How do we get from here to there?

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content: The document notes that answers to these questions will carry their own security and privacy implications, to be addressed in RFCs that propose solutions. The questions about discovery and trustworthiness of path properties are most security-relevant. For instance, if endpoints can discover that a path includes specific nodes, an adversary might forge or intercept path property information. If path properties are trustworthy but stale, endpoints might make poor decisions. Multipath communication to resist surveillance (mentioned in Question 5) requires careful protocol design to avoid creating linkable identifiers across paths.
sections.eli5: If endpoints can see the path, bad actors could lie about it or track which paths you pick. Protocols need to make sure that information is real and that attackers cannot figure out which packets belong together.
